data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A test constrains its subject when it is installed before the code that could pass it is written, and the installation ritual forces failures to be visible as failures rather than silently absorbed by the test's own guard logic; the 3-of-26 result is the residue of tests whose guards checked declared data rather than added behavior, so they described what the author already believed instead of constraining what the code could become.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the mutation is syntactic rather than behavioral, declared-data guards may constrain adequately.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the registry is rebuilt after each mutation instead of before, installation-first ordering is irrelevant.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the author writes the test and the mutation in the same session, the test is more likely to describe the author's current belief than to constrain the code.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the test suite is small enough that a human reviews every passing case, the guard ontology matters less.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Installation-first ordering creates a registry of expected failures. When a mutation lands, the registry forces a decision: either the mutation is declared as the new passing state or the test must fire. Tests that only inspect declared structure (names, signatures, literal fields) cannot see behavioral mutations, so they report 'caught' without constraining anything. The 3-of-26 survivors are exactly the cases where the guard's ontology (declared data) is disjoint from the mutation's ontology (added behavior).","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
